scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): backs honest advice while arguing that a duty to dissuade would do more harm than good; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Schools naturally want to protect their students from wasting years on a hopeless path.
Some people argue that educational institutions have a responsibility to dissuade students from pursuing fields in which they are unlikely to succeed.
I agree that schools should advise students honestly, but I believe a duty to dissuade them would do more harm than good.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why honest advice is good

sentences.text: First, schools do have a duty to give students honest and realistic advice.
Good guidance can save a student from years of struggle in a direction with little hope.
For example, a counsellor who gently shares the true difficulty of a field helps a student plan wisely.
This shows that realistic advice can be a genuine kindness rather than a discouragement.
Honest information about a field's demands lets students make better-informed choices.
Schools also have limited places that should not be filled carelessly.
To this extent, schools rightly owe students honest guidance.
Second, however, an active duty to dissuade students would often be mistaken and harmful.
Schools frequently cannot tell who will succeed, since effort and passion can overcome early weakness.
Consider the many famous achievers who were once judged hopeless by their own teachers.
Such cases show that discouraging students risks robbing the world of their later success.
A duty to dissuade could also crush ambition and push young people away from their dreams.
It would turn schools into gatekeepers deciding futures far too early.
Guidance should open doors for students, not close them before they have truly tried.
In conclusion, schools should give students honest advice about their chances of success.
But a responsibility to actively dissuade them would stifle ambition and often prove wrong.
The better role is to inform and support students while leaving the final choice in their hands.
